direction_summaries.explanation: It appears the feature is “lighting up” on subword pieces that serve as the connective or completing morpheme of a multi‐token word. In other words, the high‐activation segments mark the internal “glue” or affix that signals the model should complete a compound or morphologically segmented word (as in “integrate” → “inte‐GR‐ate”, “procur a” → “cur”, “lot” in an informal phrase, etc.), whereas without it the continuation becomes a generic “row.”

The sentence 'hello world' shows a smooth, unsegmented tokenization without any internal glues.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears the feature is “lighting up” on subword pieces that serve as the connective or completing morpheme of a multi‐token word. In other words, the high‐activation segments mark the internal “glue” or affix that signals the model should complete a compound or morphologically segmented word (as in “integrate” → “inte‐GR‐ate”, “procur a” → “cur”, “lot” in an informal phrase, etc.), whereas without it the continuation becomes a generic “row.”

The activation for 'flower' remained generic, with no internal morpheme lighting up.

direction_summaries.explanation: This feature activates when the model detects a sentence‐ or clause‐terminating punctuation mark (typically a period or similar delimiter) that signals the end of one thought and the beginning of another. In doing so it conditions the next-token prediction—ensuring that the following token fits a sentence‐initial context (e.g. proper capitalization and expected syntax)—whereas without the feature the model reverts to an anomalous, context–inappropriate continuation (e.g. “abad”).

The sun set quickly. Next, the stars appeared.
The concert was amazing. Finally, the encore began.
